headline: With a distinct dynamic value per element, next-yak compiles it to a CSS custom property so the class stays static, while every hash-and-inject library generates a fresh class per element and pays serialize-plus-hash a thousand times.

microbench.why: next-yak lifts the per-element value into a `--var` on a static class, so no class is regenerated — the css-prop lane emits a plain element with only the variable write (0.603 ms/1k), tying `vanilla`. The styled lane keeps a `Yak` wrapper around that same var write (1.18 ms/1k), which is why the css-prop form doubles it. Everything that names the class from the value collapses: `goober` recompiles and re-hashes per element (5.60 ms/1k), `styled-components`' `generateAndInjectStyles` fires 1000 times (4.35 ms/1k), and `panda` runs its style-prop serializer per element (3.31 ms/1k).

autocannon.why: The static-class-plus-var lanes serve most requests because each request only writes variables; the class-per-value libraries re-run their naming pipeline per request and fall to `goober` 169 req/s and `styled-components` 210 req/s.

attribution.why: The css-prop lane's library slice is 0.139 ms — the value is a variable write, nothing to hash — versus the styled lane's 0.421 ms for the surviving `Yak` wrapper. The naming libraries carry the whole cost in their slice: `goober` 4.71 ms (its object-to-CSS compile plus hash per element), `styled-components` 3.27 ms; `panda`'s style-props route it to component self-time, 3.27 ms of a 4.54 ms render.

hydrate.why: The var-based lanes hydrate at ~47-48 ms with the sheet already in the HTML. The distinct-value workload wrecks the naming runtimes on the client: `goober` reaches 1240 ms rebuilding a thousand cached rules, `styled-components` and `emotion` ~115 ms — the class-per-value pattern is at its worst when a client has to reconstruct every one.

inp.why: The interaction touches one element, so most lanes land at ~7-8 ms within the interaction spread — a tie that even `styled-components` joins because a single-element update regenerates only one class. `panda` (15.1 ms) and `goober` (18.6 ms) stay slow, still walking their per-element style path on the re-render.

mount.why: Mounting a thousand distinct values, the var lanes stay near the react-dom floor (~59-64 ms) because the sheet is static; `goober` mounts in 1215 ms building every rule at first paint, `emotion` 110 ms and `styled-components` 112 ms.

renderTiming.why: One style recalc for every approach — the per-element `--var` updates recalc in a single batch just like static classes, so the css-var route adds no paint penalty. The styleMs spread (0.069-0.157 ms) is sub-millisecond.

payload.why: next-yak ships one static class plus inline `--var` values (5.24-6.32 kB gz), so the markup grows only by the variable strings. The class-per-value libraries inline a thousand distinct rules or class names: `styled-components` 35.3 kB, `emotion` 39.1 kB — 5.6-6.2× the css-prop lane.

nsweep.why: As distinct values scale to 4000, the var lanes stay flat with react-dom (~2.6 ms) while the naming cost compounds one class per element — `styled-components` 18.9 ms, `goober` 139 ms, the steepest curve in the run.

crossCase: `dyn-translate` is the naive end of the dynamic-value trio. It uses each library's natural dynamic API with no hand-tuning, which is exactly why the hash libraries suffer — nobody has split the static rule from the changing value. In `dyn-fair` alongside, developers hand-write that split (static class plus inline style) to reach parity; in `dyn-inline` the value is a plain inline style from the start. next-yak needs neither workaround: it compiles the css-var split as a feature, so its number barely moves across all three.
